 Well, it's official: there are two new kids on the block. The new MacBook Pro M6 and the MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen are finally here. If you've been waiting to upgrade, or are looking to pick up your first-ever MacBook, now's the time to do it. Pre-orders are live , and we've even found a trick to help you save up to $1,400 on the OLED model .
 As someone who owns a MacBook and uses one for work, and coincidentally tests the latest and greatest peripherals, I know that your setup isn't complete until you buy the right accessories. I couldn't get on with my work without my trusty mouse, keyboard, monitor, and other gadgets.
 Whether you're after a new mechanical keyboard or even a touch-sensitive one whose keycaps double as a trackpad, a pair of earbuds, or need a USB-C dock for more connectivity, I've got you covered. I've rounded up what I believe are the best accessories (and gadgets) to make the most of your new MacBook Pro M6 or OLED.
 New MacBook Pro pre-orders 
 OLED touchscreen
 MacBook Pro OLED 14-inch: $2,899 at Apple The MacBook Pro OLED is one of the biggest MacBook releases in recent years. It can be configured with an M5 Pro (from $2,899) or M5 Max (from $4,499) CPU and packs a 14.2-inch PROLED XDR touchscreen display with 3024 x 1986 resolution, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB SSD. You also get three Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C) ports, HDMI port, and an SDXC slot. The laptop will be available on November 6. 
 View Deal 
 M6 chip
 MacBook Pro M6 14-inch: $1,999 at Amazon Power users looking for a boost in performance should opt for the new 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro. This powerful laptop sports Apple's M6 chip for blazing-fast performance at home or on the go.
 View Deal 
 Monitor 
 27-inch
 Apple Studio Display: was $1,569 now $1,519 at BHPhoto There's no better monitor for your new MacBook Pro than the first-party Apple Studio Display, thanks to its excellent 12MP ultra-wide camera, fantastic six-speaker setup and gorgeous 27-inch 5K screen. It's bright and delivers accurate (and stunning) colors, too.
 Read our full Apple Studio Display review . 
 View Deal 
 27-inch
 BenQ MA270S: $999 at benq.com If you don't mind a third-party display, I can't recommend the BenQ MA270S enough. It's cheaper than the Apple Studio Display and boasts wide color coverage and excellent accuracy, making it a great choice for creatives, and it comes with an Apple-like app for customization. There’s no shortage of ports, and the Nano Gloss 5K panel is a sight to behold.
 Read my full BenQ MA270S review . 
 View Deal 
 40-inch
 Alogic Edge 5K: $1,699 at Adorama If you want more screen real estate, the Alogic Edge 40-inch 5K is an excellent choice. Boasting great color coverage and accuracy, and hosting a plethora of ports for Mac users, this monitor offers everything you could ask for. Available in Silver and Space Gray, it’ll fit right into your existing Mac-first setup, too.
 Read my full Alogic Edge 5K review . 
 View Deal 
 Keyboard 
 Touch-sensitive
 Clevetura S: $199 at Amazon The Clevetura S is an outstanding travel-friendly keyboard with touch-sensitive keycaps that turn it into a highly effective and responsive trackpad with MacBook gestures, negating the need for a separate mouse. Its scissor switches are great to type on, too.
 Read my full Clevetura S review . 
 View Deal 
 100% layout
 Keychron K10 Max: $119 at Amazon The K10 Max is a fantastic iteration of the tried-and-true Keychron formula, offering additional sound dampening, a refined mounting system, and high-performance Super Switches. A deep, thick sound and responsive keystrokes make this a great gaming option, too. It comes with macOS keycaps, making it a solid choice for Apple users.
 Read our full Keychron K10 Max review . 
 View Deal 
 75% layout
 Epomaker Glyph: was $139 now $132 at Amazon Want a keyboard that looks a bit different? The typewriter-like Epomaker Glyph (featuring macOS keycaps) is a wonderful, whimsical addition to any setup. It puts the joy back into typing. The keyboard sports a charming typewriter-like design with dual screens and customizable RGB lighting, and build quality is solid.
 Read my full Epomaker Glyph review . 
 View Deal 
 Mouse 
 Touch-sensitive
 Apple Magic Mouse (USB-C): $79 at BHPhoto There's no better mouse for the MacBook other than the Apple Magic Mouse (as long as you don't mind the very flat design). It features a Multi-Touch surface that allows you to perform gestures, and the mouse can last up to a month between charges. This model features a USB-C port. On the bottom.
 View Deal 
 Ergonomic
 BenQ INFTYLAB M Mouse PS01: $119 at BHPhoto If you want an ergonomic mouse with buttons that toggle macOS shortcuts, try the BenQ INFTYLAB M Mouse PS01. It features dual scrolling wheels, smooth tracking, and you can assign macOS gestures to its buttons. User-friendly companion software makes customization easy, too.
 Read my full BenQ INFTYLAB M Mouse PS01 review . 
 View Deal 
 Gaming
 Corsair M75 (Mac): $129 at Apple Given how powerful both the MacBook Pro M6 and OLED sound, I won't be surprised if they're great for gaming. The Corsair M75 (Mac) is a superb gaming mouse designed for macOS. This minimalist-looking mouse features 26,000 DPI sensitivity that you can change on the fly, making it suitable for all kinds of gaming titles. It’s very comfortable to use for long hours.
 Read my full Corsair M75 (Mac) review . 
 View Deal 
 Dock 
 Desk-made
 UGREEN 8-in-1 Thunderbolt 4 Docking Station: was $249 now $169 at Amazon The UGREEN 8-in-1 Thunderbolt 4 Docking Station is a must-have for those who have a desk setup. It's equipped with three Thunderbolt 4 ports (40Gbps, 15W), three USB-A ports (10Gbps), a gigabit ethernet port, and a 140W DC power port. It's great for creatives and professionals who need high transfer speeds.
 View Deal 
 Portable
 Anker 8-in-1 USB-C Hub: $53 at Amazon I couldn't live without my portable USB-C hub. The Anker 8-in-1 USB-C Hub is ideal for those on the move. It features multiple USB-C and USB-A ports, as well as HDMI 4K/60Hz ports for streaming and mirroring content. There are also two SD and microSD card slots — perfect for photographers and videographers.
 View Deal 
 Stand 
 Fixed, non-adjustable
 Twelve South Curve Stand: $59 at Apple The Twelve South Curve Stand sports a modern and minimal design that complements and enhances your MacBook and workspace. It raises your screen off the desk for improved ergonomics and airflow.
 View Deal 
 Adjustable
 Twelve South Curve Flex Stand: $79 at Apple The Twelve South Curve Flex Stand elevates your MacBook up to 22 inches and adjusts your keyboard angle from zero to 45°, resulting in a more ergonomic and comfortable viewing and typing experience. It folds flat so you can take it with you when you travel.
 View Deal 
 Earbuds 
 Open-ear
 Apple AirPods 5: $129 at Best Buy If you have an existing Apple ecosystem (iPhone, iPad, MacBook, etc.), the Apple AirPods 5 are an excellent choice. Starting from just $124, these affordable earbuds are the ideal model those on a budget. While the battery life is abysmal, the sound quality, comfort, fit, smart features, and ANC make up for it for casual users.
 Read our full Apple AirPods 5 review . 
 View Deal 
 Sealed in-ear
 Apple AirPods 3 Pro: was $249 now $199 at Amazon If you need AirPods that don't skimp on features, the AirPods Pro 3 are the ones for you. They pack useful features like heart rate monitor and Live Translation. The fit is fantastic and comfortable, and there's plenty of battery to keep them going for long listening sessions.
 Read our full Apple AirPods Pro 3 review . 
 View Deal 
 Over-ear
 Apple AirPods Max 2: was $549 now $449 at Amazon Stuffed full of AirPods Pro-esque features like Head Gestures, Live Translation, Camera Remote, and improved Siri integration, the AirPods Max 2 pack lots of smart tech features alongside sound that's rich, complex, and most importantly, fun.
 Read our full Apple AirPods Max 2 review . 
 View Deal 
 Sleeve 
 14-inch or 16-inch
 TomToc 360 Protective Sleeve: $42 at Amazon The TomToc 360 Protective Sleeve is a must-have for those who want to protect their new MacBook Pro M6 or OLED when they're traveling. With four corner protectors, resilient edges, high-density padding, and water-resistant fabric, it protects your laptop from inevitable bumps, scratches and water spills. It also has two separate compartments with several small pockets and a strap for an AirTag or key.
 View Deal 
 14-inch or 16-inch
 Rains Laptop Portfolio: $80 at Apple If you want a more low-key sleeve, the Rains Laptop Portfolio waterproof sleeve is sleek and good-looking. It features a flap closure fastened with concealed magnetic straps, and it's made of durable and smooth PU fabric.
 View Deal

 You've got yourself a MacBook Pro, and you're here to find a display that will act as the perfect companion for your desk setup. Well, after connecting Apple's Pro laptop to the latest screens that land on our desks, we've done the testing and found the best monitors for MacBook Pro.
 Apple's 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pros already come equipped with amazing Liquid Retina XDR displays, but to extend your workspace with monitors that match the rich, colorful visuals and high pixel density those screens offer raises the bar for your setup. That's why my team of experts and I have done extensive hands-on testing for picture quality, color accuracy, connectivity and more for each monitor to help you find the right fit for your desk.
 Right now, we highly recommend the Philips 27E3U7903 as the best monitor for MacBook Pro for most, as this 5K beauty ticks all the right boxes and is far less expensive than Apple's Studio Display (even though that is still a great choice). We've got more choices to put on your radar, so if you're ready to give your MacBook Pro the monitor it deserves, our guide will point you in the right direction.
 Looking for other displays from Apple's lineup of Macs? Check out our guides on the best monitors for Mac mini and the best monitors for Mac Studio , too.

 The best monitor for your MacBook Pro around
 Our expert review:
 Specifications
 Screen size: 27 inches 
 Resolution: 5120 x 2880 
 Brightness: 500 nits SDR, 600 nits HDR

 Reasons to buy

 Reasons to avoid
 - Very expensive
 - Not a huge subjective upgrade over 4K
 - Calibration could be a bit better
 The Philips 27E3U7903 takes the crown as our top pick for MacBook Pro users who want a monitor that nails modern connectivity and delivers a true high-res experience without the Apple tax. In our testing, we found it needs to be excellent across the board to justify its premium price, and the combination of practical features and 5K clarity gets it most of the way there.
 Connectivity is where the 27E3U7903 shines. With HDMI 2.1, a Thunderbolt 4 port delivering 96W of Power Delivery (enough to fully charge a MacBook Pro), plus additional Thunderbolt, USB-C, and USB-A ports, it handles single-cable docking, peripheral charging, and daisy chaining with ease. We found the built-in KVM switch and multi-port options made switching between devices and tidying up desk clutter genuinely seamless.
 On the visual front, you’re getting a 5K (5120 x 2880) panel using IPS Black tech, meaning crisp, retina-style sharpness for macOS, vibrant colors, and a punchy backlight. In hands-on use, the panel’s vibrancy and power stood out, making it suitable for everything from spreadsheets to creative work, even if it won’t quite match Apple on calibration out of the box.
 Yes, the Apple Studio Display still wins for build quality and Mac integration, but the Philips matches its resolution and undercuts it on price. So you aren’t paying for the logo.
 If you’re looking for a premium-feeling, high-resolution monitor that offers practical one-cable MacBook Pro docking, the 27E3U7903 is a strong choice. You’ll give up some of Apple’s design polish and factory calibration, but for most users after ports, clarity, and versatility, it’s the best all-rounder we’ve tested.

 Reasons to avoid
 - No cable management
 - Not all that bright
 - No KVM
 The BenQ GW2486TC Eye-Care Monitor is as budget-friendly as it gets for MacBook Pro users who just want a reliable desktop screen with a single-cable USB-C connection.
 You get 65W USB-C power delivery (enough for lighter MacBooks and most workdays), a 24-inch 1080p IPS panel, and a measured 99% sRGB color coverage. That simple yet effective combination delivers sharp enough text and reasonably accurate colors for routine tasks and light creative work.
 We used this monitor daily for a month, pairing it with various laptops and running through everything from spreadsheets to streaming media, and it made for a great screen companion. For one, the stand offers 130mm of height adjustment, 45-degree swivel, and 90-degree pivot, so it’s easy to dial in a comfortable setup. Secondly, the OSD menu is straightforward, and those eye-care modes are a genuine plus for long sessions, especially if your workday stretches late.
 Of course, you’re making clear trade-offs versus pricier options. The BenQ’s 65W power delivery is well below its 90W competition, and won’t keep a 16-inch MacBook Pro charged under heavy load. You’re also giving up 4K resolution and Thunderbolt, features you’ll others like the Apple Studio Display.
 For basic office use, though, the savings are real. If you’re after a clean, simple MacBook Pro setup on a tight budget, the GW2486TC covers the basics better than anything else we’ve tested at this price.

 Reasons to avoid

 - Mediocre stand, nothing special
 Ok, so the Dell UltraSharp U3226Q 32 4K QD-OLED monitor is far from a cheap 4K display, but it's an absolutely great monitor for creative professionals; whether you are editing photos or videos or getting deep into graphic design.
 A quantum dot 4K OLED display with "spectacular" picture quality per reviewer Collin Probst's testing, is the obvious star of the show. It's a superb panel for photo and video editing, and lends itself well for website design. A detachable shader also help reinforce this monitor's professional chops, but its gets plenty bright without needing the shade, according to Probst.
 Dell has a stellar reputation for making great displays for professionals, so this 32-inch OLED display's quality isn't a huge surprise. What is nice is that the monitor can do a lot via a single Thunderbolt port with power delivery, handy to plug into the somewhat restrained port selection of MacBook Pro laptops. But it also has a host of other ports, from HDMI 2.1 ports to USB-C and more, meaning you can build a comprehensive creator-centric desktop set up around it.
 Over to Probst to have the final word: "If you know you're looking for an absurdly nice monitor because you are a video editor, a photo editor, or a content creator in some way, and you need a high-quality one, then absolutely make sure you check this one out."

 You get a 32-inch 4K OLED panel delivers a sprawling workspace and crisp detail, making it ideal for photo editors, video colorists, designers – you name it. The display also offers 99% DCI-P3 coverage and a decent range of hardware calibration tools, including 3D LUT, ProArt calibration, and CalMAN Autocal,

 Best monitor for MacBook Pro: FAQs 
 (Image credit: Acer // Future) What is the best resolution for monitors with a MacBook Pro?
 The MacBook Pro is Apple's machine for creators, and that means having excellent visuals for photo and video editing, 3D creative work, and more. To make the most out of what you work on, 4K (3840 x 2160) resolution is the way to go. That said, if you're using your MacBook Pro for anything else, like spreadsheets, writing documents or even coding, you'll be just fine with even a 1080p display. If you're after the highest pixel density, though, 5K and upwards is what you're after. 
 What Power Delivery should the monitor have to charge my MacBook Pro?
 You'll see many monitors with Thunderbolt/USB-C Power Delivery (PD). This means you can plug your MacBook Pro into the monitor and it will charge the laptop while in use. 
 However, the right choice depends on your MacBook Pro's model and CPU. Check out the table below to see which one is right for your laptop.

 Are there any specific connectivity options that I should look for in a monitor for my MacBook Pro?
 The best monitors for a MacBook Pro will feature USB-C and/or Thunderbolt connectivity. These allow slick, single-cable connectivity that covers charging the MacBook, driving the display, and connecting peripherals. 
 Outside of that, you can find a monitor with a built-in USB-C hub that opens up several ports through the single USB-C used to send video to your monitor. Depending on the monitor, sometimes this can also be used to charge your MacBook Pro.
 Are there any monitors that are specifically designed for use with the MacBook Pro?
 Some monitors, such as the Apple Studio Display and Apple Pro Display XDR, are explicitly designed for use with Apple devices and mirror the wide color P3 gamut and Liquid Retina Display. 
 However, many high-quality monitors from other brands are also compatible with the MacBook Pro. Some monitors will work better with the MacBook Pro than others, but generally, any even semi-recent monitor will be compatible in one way or another with a MacBook Pro.
 How to choose the best monitor for MacBook Pro 
 When choosing which monitor is best for your MacBook Pro, there are a few specs and details you'll want to check.
 Not everyone will need the same specifications. For example, if you're mostly working with office apps, you may not need the broader color space coverage that's required for image or video editing. However you use your monitor, here's what we recommend looking out for.
 Resolution : macOS loves high-resolution displays. The more pixels, the better for rendering nice, clean fonts and providing plenty of image detail. Apple's own desktop displays, the Apple Pro Display XDR and Studio Display, have what's known as Retina pixel density. In practice, that means over 200 pixels per inch (PPI), which matches the screens in the MacBook Pro. Very few non-Apple displays can match that pixel density, but a 27-inch 4K display with 163 pixels per inch is a good baseline.
 Connectivity : USB-C or Thunderbolt with Power Delivery is the bare minimum when it comes to connectivity. We'd recommend at least 65W of power delivery and ideally 90W-plus for keeping your MacBook Pro fully powered. A USB hub with plenty of USB-A and USB-C ports is very desirable, too. Additional inputs like HDMI can be handy, and an Ethernet port can be useful for some office environments. The ability to daisy chain a second monitor is also an interesting option, as is a KVM switch if you're sharing the display with a second computer.
 HDR versus SDR support: HDR is a tricky technology. Many workflows don't require it. But it is becoming more widespread. A display with HDR capability tends to also offer increased colour coverage and generally improve image quality. However, the technologies that enable HDR rendering vary hugely, and some displays are much more effective than others. For that reason, unless you know your workflows require full HDR support, we recommend focusing on getting a display with good SDR performance. If it happens to also offer some HDR capability, great. But for most users, HDR probably isn't a top priority.
 Build quality and extras: It's easy to obsess over specifications like resolution and HDR performance. But the overall quality of a display and feature set can make a big difference, too. If you're paying big bucks, it's nice to have a display that feels worth the money and looks good with your laptop. Likewise, superficially lesser features like good speakers, a great webcam and a microphone array can make a big difference to the overall usability of a monitor. Having features like that built in can also help to reduce desk clutter and simplify docking and connectivity. For more extras, we've reviewed the best MacBook Pro accessories .
 How we test the best monitors for MacBook Pro 
 (Image credit: Future) Our expert team of reviewers has tested a massive range of displays, including the best monitors for photo editing and the best monitors for video editing . So, we're experienced at knowing what to look out for to help you find the best dual monitor set-up to go with your laptop.
 A decent monitor for your MacBook Pro isn't going to be cheap. So, you want to know you're making the right choice. That's why we test each display extensively. That starts with performance assessments of various aspects of image quality.
 That includes brightness, refresh rate, and pixel response. We also consider colour accuracy, viewing angles, contrast, HDR performance, latency, and last but by no means least, resolution and pixel density. Display tech is increasingly varied and complex, what with new technologies like HDR, mini-LED backlights, and OLED panels revolutionising the industry. So, we keep on top of all of that for you, helping you to understand the difference between a few edge-lit dimming zones and a real full-array deal
 Crucially, we also assess how well a display works with macOS. Once connected to a MacBook Pro, does it offer a full range of optimised scaling options, for instance? Next up is connectivity. We consider the range of ports on offer and whether single-cable docking with power delivery is included, along with USB hubs and other features like Ethernet, a KVM switch, and display daisy chaining.
 We also consider any extra features like webcams and speakers. In theory, they can add significant value. But if they're not done well, you're probably just paying for things you'll hardly ever use. You might even end up paying twice if you find you need to buy a dedicated webcam or speakers.
 Next up, there's build quality, design, and ergonomics. A monitor that looks great on the desk with your MacBook Pro is important. But good build quality matters, too. When you are investing a lot of money, you want a display to not just look good, but feel good and last the test of time.
 Then there's ergonomics. At a minimum, a robust and stable stand with a good range of adjustability, including height and tilt, is important. The ability to rotate into portrait mode can be handy, too.
 Of course, how all of those factors fit into the overall value proposition is the final measure. The MacBook Pro is a demanding machine. So, you're not going to get the best out of it with a budget display. But you can also spend a lot of money and not necessarily get a better display solution. We'll help you work out what's worth the money and what costs plenty but doesn't improve your macOS experience.

 Apple is updating two more computers to its M6 system-on-chip. The base 14-inch MacBook Pro and the iMac lineup are getting the company's latest processor ahead of tomorrow's "Pro and Tell" event in Los Angeles.
These devices are retaining the same designs that they've had for years. The computers will be available for pre-order on Wednesday at 10:10 a.m. PT (1:10 p.m. ET) and will ship on Nov. 6. The M6 in the MacBook Pro will be configured with 12 CPU cores and 12 GPU cores, alongside dual neural engines for certain on-device AI workloads. On the iMac, there will also be a cut-down option with a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU.
 (Image credit: Apple) The MacBook Pro will be configurable with up to 32GB of RAM and is being updated with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 using Apple's N1 networking chip. The iMac is also getting those networking benefits, as well as a 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet port. Like previous iMacs, the number of ports you get is tied to the chip, with two Thunderbolt 4 ports with the base chip or four with the option with more cores.
It's no surprise that Apple is pushing both of these as AI-forward machines, both with the new chips and the recently released Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features in macOS 27 Golden Gate.
The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 will start at $1,999 ($1,899 with education discount), while the iMac will begin at $1,499 ($1,449 with education discount) for the 10-core CPU/GPU configuration and $1,699 ($1,599 with education discount) for the full chip.
 Both of these new systems are being announced the day before Apple is expected to release a MacBook with an OLED touchscreen. Yesterday, in a week of announcements, Apple debuted a redesign of the iPad Mini with a thinner body and an OLED display.

 USB-C: 5Gbps or 10Gbps
 USB4: 20Gbps or 40Gbps
 Thunderbolt 3 and 4: 40Gbps
 Thunderbolt 5: 80Gbps / 120Gbps
 Our list Which ports does my MacBook have will show you how many USB-C or more likely one of Thunderbolt 3, 4 or 5 that you have.
 While a Thunderbolt 4 (TB4) dock will be enough for most casual users, if you can stretch the budget go for a TB5 dock as it will remain current for years, saving you money in the long term, and is backwards compatible with earlier versions and all the way back to USB-C. High-end professionals should always aim for Thunderbolt 5.
 The dock needs one (“ upstream “) Thunderbolt or USB-C port for connecting to and charging your laptop (although all recent MacBooks can also power via the MagSafe 3 port), and at least another (“ downstream “) to attach further devices (hard drives, external display, and others).
 The USB-C MacBook Neo has just the one data port, with the other reserved for charging. A dock with Power Delivery will greatly expand the entry-level Mac laptop.
 For more detail, read our Thunderbolt 5 vs Thunderbolt 4 vs Thunderbolt 3 vs USB4 explainer .
 Add external displays to your MacBook
 If you use your laptop as your principal computer, attaching at least one larger display to create a hybrid desktop/laptop setup, with a keyboard and mouse, will boost your productivity. You can turn that 13in MacBook’s cramped screen real-estate into an iconic iMac-sized 27in or even larger screen by adding an extra display—or connect two or even four large monitors to extend your screen across your whole desk. Take a look at our recommended best monitors and displays for Mac and also the best portable monitors for Mac .
 You’ll get two or more Extended mode screens (where the screen extends beyond what you can see on the laptop screen) using a Thunderbolt connection (or DisplayPort/HDMI). Natively over mere USB-C, Macs can connect to only one external display in Extended mode, as opposed to Mirrored mode (which replicates exactly what you get on the laptop screen) but DisplayLink is third-party software that allows some docks to extend to up to four screens on even the most basic Mac. DisplayLink-supporting docks are also the only way that non-Pro/Max M1 and M2 MacBooks can connect more than one external display.
 More explained: we cover more on Mac docking stations and external displays at the end of this feature below our recommendations.
 Do I need a docking station?
 With three TB4 or TB5 and an HDMI port, a MacBook with a Max chip could connect to up to four external displays without the need for a dock, although such a power user would likely require extra Thunderbolt and other ports for more devices to make up for using all the laptop ports for multiple monitors. See below our list of recommended docking stations for more detail on the external display options with each recent MacBook .
 All docks come with a bunch of USB ports: some old-school USB-A and newer, more capable USB-C . MacBook Pros also have an SD card reader . Although this card reader is rated as UHS-II (312MBps), Apple has pegged it back at 250MBps, so for the fastest speeds (and a microSD slot if you need one), a dock will likely be a better choice for memory-card use if it is rated at UHS-II rather than UHS-I (104MBps).
 MacBooks also lack wired Internet access via an Ethernet port, so if you want to escape flaky Wi-Fi, buy a dock with at least Gigabit Ethernet, although you could add a Thunderbolt-to-Ethernet adapter instead if you have a spare TB port. Some later docks include faster 2.5Gb, 5Gb or even 10Gb Ethernet but you’ll need a supporting router or other device to get the benefits, although these faster Ethernet ports are backwards compatible with Gigabit so will future-proof your purchase.
 While docking stations are most often attached to MacBooks, they can be useful with a desktop Mac. The Mac mini especially can benefit from the extra ports and built-in SSD slot options. We cover these specifically in our feature on how to upgrade the Mac mini , including reviews of the best hubs and docks that fit the mini. 
 Dock or hub?
 If you need just a few extra ports, a USB-C hub or Thunderbolt hub might be your best choice—see our roundup of the best USB-C and Thunderbolt hubs for Mac . However, if you require a bunch of fast ports including Gigabit (or faster) Ethernet and multiple video ports plus more powerful charging capability, then look for a full dock that fulfils your needs. We’ve reviewed the best hubs alongside the docks.
 USB-C and Thunderbolt speeds
 Simon Jary / Foundry
 • USB and Thunderbolt speeds explained 
 USB PD: Power Delivery for your laptop
 Most docks can charge the connected MacBook, so look for the right Power Delivery (PD) rating that suits your laptop. You can’t over-power a MacBook so the simplest advice is to aim as high as you can. 70W will be more than enough to fast-charge a MacBook Air but go for 85W or more (PD 3.0) for a MacBook Pro, and 140W (PD 3.1) for the top-end 16-inch Pro.
 We’ve got more detailed advice on recommended MacBook charging speeds below our list of docks.
 Best docks for Mac 2026
 Here we list the Thunderbolt and USB-C docks that we have reviewed and tested. Read the descriptions for details on all the features and functions offered by each docking station.
 We start with the latest Thunderbolt 5 docks as they offer the most but docks with TB4 might well be all you need and often (not always) come in cheaper. The benefit of buying a Thunderbolt 5 dock now—even if your Mac doesn’t have it—is that it’s backwards compatible and future proofs you for your next Mac purchase.
 You can save money by choosing a Thunderbolt 4 or even USB-C docking station, the best of which are also reviewed in this chart.

We’d have preferred a bit more power output from the USB-C ports, but the Sonnet Echo Thunderbolt 5 docks come with the latest and greatest connectivity standards (including 10Gb Ethernet), and will turn any pro MacBook into a powerful and flexible multi-screen workstation.

 If you desire the ultimate in MacBook docking stations, the CalDigit TS5 Plus has just about everything you need—indeed probably more than you need. Alongside super-fast Thunderbolt 5 you get an incredible number of top-end ports including 10Gb Ethernet and an incredible 330W power supply. Only iVanky’s FusionDock Ultra and Max 2, both reviewed below, have more ports.
 Somehow CalDigit has included an incredible clearly labelled 20 ports into the compact dock—all of which can be used simultaneously—including ten 10Gbps USB ports (five USB-C and five USB-A), the fastest Ethernet available, top-rated card readers and audio ports front and back. There are three 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5 ports: one upstream to connect to your computer and two downstream for speedy data-transfer devices.
 CalDigit has sacrificed a possible third downstream TB5 port for a dedicated DisplayPort in the knowledge that most dock users run at least one external display and so the extra TB5 port would be used for a monitor connection anyway. Depending on the display capabilities of your MacBook, the maximum resolution is 8K at a 60Hz refresh rate, with a possible refresh rate of 240Hz for 4K or 500Hz for 1080p HD.
 Advances in the top-end M5 processors mean that a MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip can now respectively attach three or four external displays from the TS5 Plus. Standard M5, M4 Pro and M4 Max and lower are still restricted to two external displays.
 The TS5 Plus is the first dock with dual 10Gbps USB controllers, one controller for the front ports and one for the ports at the back of the dock for increased USB bandwidth. Each of the USB ports offers 7.5W of power except the front-facing 36W USB-C port. The two downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports also offer 36W. As it has the highest power supply of any dock tested here (330W), all can output at a maximum at the same time—something that’s not possible with most other docks.

 While the CalDigit TS5 Plus has just about everything you need, the iVanky FusionDock Ultra probably does have everything and a whole bunch more. It boasts a frankly ridiculous 26 ports, including six Thunderbolt 5 thanks to its dual-chip architecture. This dock is for high-end Mac professionals who need maximum connectivity, especially those running multiple high-resolution displays, fast storage and 10Gb networking all at once.
 The advantage this dock has over other Thunderbolt 5 docks is its dual Thunderbolt 5 chips, making it effectively two docks in one case. Using two upstream Thunderbolt connections also provides significantly more bandwidth, avoiding the bottlenecks that often occur with single-port docks. The downside is that you must use two of your Mac’s Thunderbolt ports to use the FusionDock Ultra. If only one cable is connected, some ports on the dock will not function.
 The Ultra can natively deliver up to four external displays—a feat that usually takes a docking station that requires third-party DisplayLink compression software to be installed on the Mac. While TB5 docks can run four displays when connected to a top-end M5 Max MacBook, the fourth display must be daisy-chained off the third as other docks have only three downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports.  Mac docking stations and external displays
 Baseus
 While Apple’s MacBooks featuring the company’s own M-series Silicon chips are super speedy compared to the models sporting Intel processors, models with plain (non-Pro or -Max) M1 and M2 chips come with an incredible limitation: they don’t support more than one external display in Extended Mode even via their Thunderbolt ports. Plain M3 MacBooks can support two displays but only with their lids closed. The MacBook Neo uses a different A18 Pro chip and has the same single-monitor limitation as the plain M1 and M2.
 This limitation means that when using any docking station, M1/M2 and Neo MacBook users cannot extend their desktop over two or more displays, and will be limited to either dual Mirrored displays or one external display—although adding third-party DisplayLink or InstantView software to the Mac and connecting to a dedicated USB-C dock will allow you to add more than one external monitor to an M1, M2 or M3 MacBook . Follow that link for our roundup of the best USB-C DisplayLink docks , and we’ve included our favorite in our roundup above.
 In the example above, standard M1/M2/Neo Macs would require DisplayLink to achieve Extended Mode 2. M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro/Max and standard M3/M4/M5 onwards can natively work in that mode without DisplayLink but would require it for three or more extended screens. M5 Pro supports three screens, and M5 Max supports four, without requiring DisplayLink.
 Above, we’ve listed the native external display options for each MacBook. Thunderbolt 5 docks should support up to four 6K displays if you own an M5 Max-chip MacBook Pro.
 While some docking stations promise support for 8K displays, Macs are limited to 6K support via the dock. Macs with an M2/M3/M4 Pro or Max chip can support an 8K display at 60Hz but only when it is connected via the Mac’s own HDMI port and not any port on the dock.
 Dock, hub or dongle: Whole lotta ports
 You need one (“ upstream “) Thunderbolt or USB-C port for connecting to and charging your laptop (although the 14/16in MacBooks can also power via the MagSafe port), and likely at least another (“ downstream “) to attach further devices (hard drives, external display, and others).
 There are many inexpensive USB-C dongles/hubs that let you add more devices to a MacBook (see our roundup of the best USB-C adapters for Macs ) or a Thunderbolt hub offering a few extra ports might be all your need, but for maximum flexibility check out a docking station that takes care of all your extra port requirements, and allows you to simply attach it to your laptop with just one cable when you get to the office or come home.
 Docks aren’t just for MacBooks. Mac mini (2018 and later) and iMac (2017 and later) owners may also consider expanding their ports with a Thunderbolt docking station.
 The inclusion of an SD or microSD card reader isn’t just for camera buffs. It’s a convenient and affordable way to add storage to your laptop setup. We found a 512GB Samsung Evo microSD card on Amazon for around $100 in the US and under £100  in the UK. That’s a very cheap way of adding half a terabyte of portable storage. For more details read up on our best microSD cards .
 Some of the docks reviewed above include an integrated SSD enclosure that lets you add up to 8TB of fast storage to your connected MacBook.
 Charging the laptop
 While the MacBook Neo can get by on 20W Power Delivery (PD), the M1/M2/M3/M4/M5 MacBook Air requires a PD charger with at least 30W power, but you can fast-charge an M2 and later Air with a charger rated at over 70W. You’ll need 67W for the 13-inch MacBook Pro and 70W for the 14-inch MBP (with 8-, 10-, 11-or 12-core CPU), 96W for 14-inch MBP (with 12- or 14-core CPU), and 96W (preferably 140W) for the 16-inch MBP. The older 15in MacBook Pro requires a 87W PD charger.
 If you own a larger MacBook Pro, buy a dock with a PD (Power Delivery) potential of at least 85W if you can. USB PD 3.0 maxes at 100W, while USB PD 3.1 can support up to 240W of power. The 16-inch MacBook Pro requires 140W to fast-charge, so owners of that laptop should look for a PD 3.1 charger.
 If you just need a spare charger, we’ve tested the best MacBook chargers for you.
 Other dock options
 Here we concentrate on Thunderbolt docks, but also include cheaper USB-C docks—which Thunderbolt MacBooks can use, but at the cost of reduced bandwidth and display limitations. We’ve also included our favorite Thunderbolt hubs for smaller and cheaper alternatives. For more non-Thunderbolt USB-C-only docks check out Tech Advisor’s roundup of the best USB-C docking stations for laptops . Tech Advisor also reviews all the available Thunderbolt 4 docks .
 Now think about a stand to go alongside the dock
 These MacBook docking stations look and work great with a laptop stand, and we’ve also tested some MacBook-friendly stands that lack all the extra ports but keep your MacBook/Air/Pro upright and out of the way: further saving valuable desk space, reducing clutter, keeping your laptop cool, and saving it from spills.

 We've extensively benchmarked the best Thunderbolt and USB-C docks in 2026 and have compiled a list of the best models on the market here. There used to be a time when laptops would come with a bevy of ports to satisfy most of your connectivity needs. While some larger, desktop-replacement laptops still have a relatively large number of ports, ultrabooks have mostly reduced the number of ports to the bare minimum to save space and reduce weight.
 While these efforts result in laptops that are thin and light, if you want to connect a wide variety of devices, including external monitors, you’ll need a dongle or a dock. While dongles are fine for connecting a single peripheral, docks are handy for connecting a variety of devices while simultaneously charging your laptop.
 The two most common connectivity options for modern docks are USB-C and Thunderbolt . Nearly every laptop on the market has at least one USB-C port available, which opens up a wealth of possibilities for connecting everything from an external monitor to an external hard drive to webcams to gaming mice. Thunderbolt ports are less common, particularly the latest Thunderbolt 5 standard, but these docks give you the option for even more ports and faster maximum transfer speeds while supporting higher-resolution monitors.

 Best Thunderbolt and USB-C Docks for Laptops Shopping Tips 
 Thunderbolt or USB-C? 
 A lot of this will come down to the type of ports available on your laptop. If you have a free Thunderbolt port, a Thunderbolt 4 or Thunderbolt 5 dock will give you a wider array of port options and higher maximum transfer speeds. 
 If you don’t have a Thunderbolt port, your only option is a USB-C dock. However, if you have a Thunderbolt port and want to go with a more economical option, you can still use a USB-C dock. The reverse is not true, however, as a Thunderbolt dock won’t work via a standard USB-C port.
 Should you go with an internal M.2 slot?
 For those who’d like to add fast SSD storage to your system, a Thunderbolt 5 dock with an internal M.2 slot is a viable option. If you already have an old M.2 SSD lying around, you can simply pop it into an internal bay and be up and running in minutes. Not only is the SSD tucked away, out of sight, but you also don’t have to take up a USB-C or Thunderbolt port with an external adapter or dedicated portable SSD.
 Wired networking speeds
 Many people who purchase a Thunderbolt/USB-C dock for a laptop do so for desktop use, i.e., turning their laptop into a productivity powerhouse with an external monitor. With this in mind, it’s nice to have a wired Ethernet connection for faster, more consistent performance. Thunderbolt 4 docks usually max out at 2.5 Gbps, while Thunderbolt 5 docks max out at 10 Gbps. Most USB-C docks are limited to 1 GbE speeds.
 Windows vs Mac support
 Be careful and READ the specs BEFORE committing to a Thunderbolt dock. Not all docks are created equal, and external monitor support will vary depending on what hardware and operating system you’re using. For example, the Ivanky FusionDock Ultra only works on Macs, and further restrictions limit it to only Apple Silicon Macs.
 Monitor support can be especially tricky. For example, the CalDigit TS5 Plus supports triple monitors on M5 Max and M5 Pro Macs, but not on M4 Pro/M4 Max or older Macs. On the other hand, Windows PCs have no trouble supporting three external monitors over Thunderbolt 5. Only an M5 Max Mac can support four external monitors simultaneously.

 Who is it for?  MacBook owners looking to connect multiple displays and fast Thunderbolt 5 devices.
 Who shouldn’t buy it?  People who want to use their MacBook screen at the same time as external monitors.
 Most docking stations sit or stand separately from the host laptop that connects via a single USB-C or Thunderbolt cable. You want to hide them and their snaky cables away from sight.
 The Brydge ProDock takes a different approach, being a vertical dock that you slide your closed MacBook into so that it connects with the dock’s built-in connector to make every port, display, and connection instantly live with minimal footprint and clutter. It even features a MagSafe-compatible wireless charging pad for your iPhone.
 Brydge
 It’s a sleek dock aesthetic that puts all the tech (including your MacBook) into one compact and convenient desk placement. When you want to take your laptop away from the desk, you simply lift it out — without having to disconnect and then reconnect any cables.
 The top-end Brydge ProDock Trio reviewed here is part of a wider ProDock range, starting with the new entry-level ProDock Solo , and a refreshed Thunderbolt 4 ProDock Duo . Packing Thunderbolt 5, the ProDock Trio delivers the highest bandwidth and multi-display performance for power users.
 Simon Jary
 What ports does the Brydge ProDock Trio have?
 The Brydge ProDock Trio includes four Thunderbolt 5 ports, one USB-C port, three USB-A ports, 2.5Gb Ethernet, an SD card reader, a 3.5mm audio jack and 140W host charging.
 The Thunderbolt 5 ports are fully backwards compatible with lesser Thunderbolt 4 MacBook Pro and Air models. While these won’t be able to take advantage of TB5’s full 80/120Gbps, the dock will remain useful to you when you upgrade to a Thunderbolt 5 MacBook. Thunderbolt 5 will be the mainstay connection for Macs for the foreseeable future so buying in now is a sensible decision.
 If you simply don’t need such bandwidth you can save some money by opting for the Thunderbolt 4 ProDock Duo that hosts a similar rack of dock ports.
 ProDock Trio
 One upstream Thunderbolt 5 connector (80Gbps, 140W) inside sleeve
 Three downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports (80Gbps, 15W) at rear
 1x USB-C (10Gbps, 5.5W) on side 1
 2x USB-A (10Gbps, 5.5W) at rear
 1x USB-A (10Gbps, 5.5W) on side 2
 Ethernet (2.5Gb) at rear
 SD Card Reader (4.0, UHS-II, 312MBps) on side 1
 MagSafe Compatible Phone Charger (10W) on front
 3.5mm combo audio jack on side 2
 180W power supply 
 Missing are video ports, with the three downstream Thunderbolt ports taking on the display connection jobs. This is a flexible approach with the caveat that you may have to add adapter cables if your monitor demands either DisplayPort or HDMI.
 While a dedicated DisplayPort or HDMI port can save you having to invest in adapter cables, most modern monitors include USB-C or Thunderbolt connections, and leaving the choice up to the user means the dock’s Thunderbolt ports can be used for either video or other devices as required. An HDMI port when your display has a USB-C connection is likely a wasted one, and when there are only eleven each port needs to count.
 On one side there’s a 10Gbps USB-C port and fast SD card reader. Simon Jary
 The other side has an audio jack and a 10Gbps USB-A port. Simon Jary
 And because the MacBook connects vertically you still have access to the laptop’s own HDMI port, plus a Thunderbolt and SD card reader slot at the top.
 There is one extra USB-C port (10Gbps) alongside the faster Thunderbolts (80Gbps). It would have been a bonus for this port to have a higher power output than its mere 5.5W. Fast-charging an iPhone or iPad requires at least 18W.
 Brydge
 There’s a handy MagSafe-compatible wireless charging pad on the dock, but it’s also relatively slow at 10W. A certified MagSafe or Qi2 charging pad would have increased this to 15W or even 25W.
 There are three legacy USB-A ports (10Gbps) that should be plenty in today’s USB-C-dominated world. With the USB-C port and the three downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports, there are enough connections for most users.
 With fast 2.5Gb Ethernet now the norm on top-end docking stations, it’s appreciated here. It will work with the more standard Gigabit Ethernet (1GbE), and future-proofs your investment for when you upgrade network speeds.
 Brydge
 Design and build
 One of the reasons you’ll be considering any of the ProDock models is the tidy vertical arrangement. It’s a convenient design if you’re not planning on using the MacBook’s own screen. In my home office I have a dual-stacked monitor while my closed MacBook lies flat on the desk taking up too much of what’s left of the desk when it’s hosting the large screens, a keyboard and mouse—plus my glass of water and coffee cup.
 The ProDock entirely takes away the MacBook’s desk hogging.
 At the point of purchase you choose the Sleeve Adapter (the part the laptop fits into) for your size MacBook from a choice of four: MacBook Air (13in or 15in, M2-M5), MacBook Pro (14in or 16in, M1-M5). Even though it won’t get the full benefit of Thunderbolt 5, a MacBook Air can still use the ProDock Trio, although a Duo probably makes more sense.
 You screw this onto the dock, with screws and screwdriver included. There are little padded stickers for the MacBook’s USB-C ports to protect from frequent insertion and removal.
 The MacBook fits in only one way so you can’t choose which side of ports sticks out the top and is still available for use.
 That means the MagSafe 3 power connector can’t be used, but isn’t required as the dock supplies the power via the Thunderbolt connection. But it also means one of the MacBook’s three TB ports goes unused. HDMI, SD slot and one TB port remain available for use at the top, depending on your MacBook model, of course.
 With the MacBook out of the sleeve, the ProDock is 127mm tall. Including the magnetic wireless charging section, it is 203mm long. Its width depends on which sleeve is in use for your MacBook model’s size.
 Brydge
 What display setups can the Brydge ProDock Trio handle?
 Any dock user wants to hook up to an external monitor, and this becomes essential when your MacBook’s lid has to be closed to fit in the ProDock’s sleeve. You can connect up to three displays from the dock if your Mac supports it.
 Macs with an M5 Pro or Max can handle up to three 6K displays at 144Hz (DSC) or two 8K at 60Hz with this dock. M1/M2/M3 Max, plus all M4/M5 variants, support up to two 8K displays at 60Hz. M1/M2/M3 Pro support up to two 6K displays at 60Hz with DSC-enabled monitors; two 4K/60Hz without DSC.
 MacBook Air models with M3/M4/M5 chip support up to two 6K/60Hz displays (DSC). MacBook Air models with a base M1/M2 chip support only a single 4K display. The MacBook Neo has a similar limitation but doesn’t fit any of the ProDock models.
 MacBook Pro users can still use the exposed HDMI port and keep one of the dock’s Thunderbolt 5 ports free for another device.
 Brydge
 How much power can the ports output?
 The upstream Thunderbolt 5 port can supply up to 140W of power (PD 3.1) to your connected laptop, which is enough to fast-charge even the top-end 16-inch MacBook Pro.
 The dock is less able, however, at outputting power to other devices, which might be because of its now rather average 180W power supply. With a possible 140W going to the MacBook, there might not be a whole lot left for other devices. If the laptop is taking just 100W or less (as is likely), the 180W should be fine.
 None of the Thunderbolt ports can deliver more than 15W of power, which is enough to charge a connected iPhone or iPad but not fast-charge them. The USB-C port is rated at just 5.5W, which should be fine for your AirPods case or Apple Watch. USB-A isn’t up to fast-charging so its low charging output is less of an issue.
 If Brydge had included a 20W or 30W USB-C port or allowed for one of the Thunderbolt ports at that power output, and then boosted the power supply to 240W, this dock would better suit pro users in a studio situation.
 ProDock family
 If you don’t need Thunderbolt’s full 80Gbps bandwidth, Brydge has two cheaper vertical models for you to consider.
 Brydge ProDock Solo ( $229 )
 Brydge
 With an HDMI 2.0 port, this single-display dock is aimed more at MacBook Air users. The MacBook Neo’s USB-C port configuration doesn’t yet fit a ProDock sleeve.
 One upstream USB-C connector (10Gbps, 90W)
 2x USB-C (5Gbps, 5.5W)
 3x USB-A (5Gbps, 5.5W)
 Ethernet (1Gb)
 SD Card Reader (3.0, UHS-I, 104MBps) on side 1

 135W power supply

 Brydge
 This Thunderbolt 4 model also lacks some of the Trio’s faster port variations, such as 2.5Gb Ethernet and 10Gbps USB-C in favor of slower versions but costs less. Unless you are planning on connecting to a fast network or connecting a speedier storage drive, these aren’t automatically limitations.
 One upstream Thunderbolt 4 connector (40Gbps, 98W)

 Is the Brydge ProDock Trio worth its price?
 The ProDock Trio Thunderbolt 5 Dock is priced at $459 but is currently discounted to $399 . It is planned to be available via Amazon in the coming weeks, but not on international Amazon until 2027 so non-US customers may encounter higher shipping and custom fees.
 Thunderbolt 5 docking stations start at $300, so you are paying a premium for the space-saving and pleasing vertical design and required sleeve.
 It’s difficult to compare it to other Thunderbolt 5 docking stations as its design is so unique. If you want dedicated display ports and more powerful ports, check out the options in our roundup of the best Thunderbolt docks.
 If you’re stuck choosing between the $399 ProDock Trio and $359 ProDock Duo, at the current pricing we recommend the Trio if you can go the extra mile. You get Thunderbolt 5 and 2.5Gb Ethernet (both useful for future-proofing even if you don’t need them now), faster USB-C, and higher power output (180W vs 135W).
 Should you buy the Brydge ProDock Trio?
 If you desire the vertical format for space-saving or purely aesthetic reasons, the sleek Thunderbolt 5 Brydge ProDock Trio is a neat, unique solution that adds a tidy stack of speedy connections to your MacBook without messing up your desk.

 The right dock for a 2026 MacBook depends less on the number of ports printed on the box than on the Mac’s chip, display limit, host protocol and the kind of video connection you need. The M5 MacBook Air has Thunderbolt 4; M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro models have Thunderbolt 5. A Thunderbolt 5 dock can work with a Thunderbolt 4 Mac, but it cannot make that Mac operate at Thunderbolt 5 speeds.
 For most MacBook Air owners, a good Thunderbolt 4 or USB-C dock is sufficient. Thunderbolt 5 becomes more compelling for an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro with several high-resolution monitors, fast storage or 10Gb Ethernet. If you need more displays than Apple supports natively, DisplayLink is the specialist option—but it requires software and has important streaming limitations.

 1. CalDigit TS5 Plus: best premium dock for a demanding MacBook Pro 
 The CalDigit TS5 Plus is the most expansive option here. It combines three Thunderbolt 5 ports with a large collection of fast USB ports, 10Gb Ethernet and UHS-II card readers. The upstream Thunderbolt 5 connection can deliver up to 140W to the host Mac, while each of the two downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports can provide up to 36W.
 Its port selection includes five USB-C 10Gbps ports, five USB-A 10Gbps ports, DisplayPort 2.1, 10Gb Ethernet, UHS-II SD and microSD, front 3.5mm combo audio and rear audio in/out. A 330W power supply is included.
 Popular on Amazon
 CalDigit TS5 Plus - Thunderbolt 5 Docking Station, 20-Ports, 10GbE LAN | PCIe based 10GbE LAN, Dual USB Controllers, 120 Gbps Bandwidth Boost, Two 8K @ 60Hz, 140W Dedicated Host Charging, 330W PSU 
 20 Ports of Extreme Connectivity - The TS5 Plus includes 3x 80Gb/s Thunderbolt 5 ports, 5x USB-A 10Gb/s ports, 5x USB-C 10Gb/s ports, DisplayPort 2.1, SD 4.0 & microSD 4.0 UHS-II card readers, 10Gb Ethernet, and 3 x audio ports.
 More Power than Ever - The TS5 Plus host charging port provides up to 140W of dedicated power delivery, ideal for laptops such as the 16” M3/M4/M5 Pro & Max series MacBook Pro that charge at 140W. The included 330W power supply allows sustained power delivery at all times from the host charging port as well as all of the remaining ports. The downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports and one of the front USB-C ports can provide up to 36W of dedicated power delivery for accessories.
 Flexible Display Configurations - The TS5 Plus on macOS devices can connect up to Dual 6K 60Hz displays, or even Dual 8K 60Hz displays on Macs that support those resolutions. Up to Triple 6K 60Hz displays are supported on M5 Pro & Max only. Up to Quad 6K 60Hz displays are supported on M5 Max only. Windows users please check your PC’s supported display compatibility.
 10 Gigabit Ethernet - 10GbE is 10X faster than traditional 1GbE found on the majority of docking stations. Connect to ultra fast 10GbE networks in order to transfer files faster than ever, or connect to 10GbE equipped NAS storage devices. *Ethernet is only supported on Thunderbolt based hosts as well as USB4 hosts that support PCIe.
 Dual USB Controllers - A unique feature of the TS5 Plus is that it includes Dual USB Controllers. This means that the ports on the front of the dock have one 10Gb/s USB controller for all of the attached devices, and the rear ports have a second 10Gb/s controller for the devices on the back ports. This avoids any bottlenecks when multiple high speed USB devices are connected.
 $499.99 
 Buy on Amazon 
 This is a particularly strong match for an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro used with multiple monitors, fast external SSDs, a wired network and camera media. CalDigit specifies support for up to three displays on an M5 Pro Mac and four on an M5 Max Mac, subject to Apple’s own display limits and the chosen resolutions.
 There are two cautions. First, CalDigit lists the TS5 Plus at $499.99, but its U.S. store currently shows it as out of stock. Second, its 10Gb Ethernet and second USB controller require a Thunderbolt host or a USB4 host with PCIe support. It is not a generic dock for an ordinary USB-C laptop, tablet or phone.
 2. Plugable TBT-UDT3: best-value Thunderbolt 5 dock 
 At a listed direct price of $299.95, the Plugable TBT-UDT3 brings much of the useful Thunderbolt 5 capability to a lower price than the TS5 Plus. It has three downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports, two USB 10Gbps ports, one USB 5Gbps port, SD and microSD readers, 2.5Gb Ethernet and Thunderbolt Share.
 Plugable rates it for up to 140W host charging. On compatible Macs, it can drive up to three 6K/60Hz displays or three 4K/144Hz displays through native Thunderbolt connections. “Compatible” matters: the dock does not override the display limit of the MacBook connected to it.
 This is a sensible choice for an M5 Pro MacBook Pro owner who wants TB5 storage and multiple displays without paying for the TS5 Plus’s unusually large port collection. It is also suitable for Thunderbolt 4 and full-featured USB4 systems. It is not a universal USB-C dock, so confirm that the laptop supports Thunderbolt or the required USB4 features before buying.
 3. OWC Thunderbolt 5 Dock: best when host compatibility matters 
 OWC takes a broader approach than docks that require a Thunderbolt host. It specifies up to 80Gbps bidirectional data and up to 120Gbps video-stream performance with Thunderbolt 5, up to 40Gbps with Thunderbolt 3 or 4, and up to 40Gbps with USB4. USB4 Version 2 hosts can reach up to 80Gbps. With a generic USB-C host, OWC lists up to 10Gbps.
 That flexibility makes the OWC dock easier to recommend for a household or office with several types of computer. However, “USB-C compatible” does not mean every USB-C port will provide the same display or data behavior. The host USB-C port must support video output—normally DisplayPort Alt Mode—for a dock-connected monitor to work.

 It also supports up to 140W host power delivery and is backward-compatible with Thunderbolt 3 and Thunderbolt 4. It is a good fit when you want a Thunderbolt 5 dock for a newer MacBook Pro but do not want to rule out older Thunderbolt systems or a USB-C computer later.
 4. Anker Prime 14-in-1: best for HDMI and DisplayPort monitors 
 The Anker Prime 14-in-1 Thunderbolt 5 Dock is convenient for desks built around conventional monitors. Instead of requiring every display to connect through a downstream Thunderbolt port and an adapter, it provides one HDMI 2.1 output and one DisplayPort 2.1 output.
 The rest of the specification includes an upstream TB5 port with up to 140W, two downstream TB5 ports, three USB-A 10Gbps ports, two USB-C 10Gbps ports sharing up to 45W, 2.5Gb Ethernet, SD and microSD readers and a front 3.5mm combo audio jack.
 The trade-off is expansion: there are only two downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports, fewer than the Plugable and WAVLINK models. The card readers are UHS-I, rated at up to 104MB/s in the reviewed specification, so photographers moving large batches of footage will get better throughput from a dock with UHS-II readers, such as the CalDigit.
 Macworld reviewed the dock at $399.99 and recorded a best-price snapshot of $319.99 at one retailer. Prices change, so treat those figures as reference points rather than fixed pricing.
 5. WAVLINK Thunderbolt 5 Dock: lower-cost native Thunderbolt 5 
 The WAVLINK model is worth considering when downstream Thunderbolt ports are more useful to you than built-in HDMI or DisplayPort. It provides four Thunderbolt 5 ports, four USB-A 10Gbps ports, 2.5Gb Ethernet, UHS-II SD and microSD readers, a 3.5mm audio jack, up to 140W host charging and a 230W power supply.
 There is no dedicated HDMI or DisplayPort output. Monitors connect to the downstream Thunderbolt ports using the appropriate USB-C, Thunderbolt, HDMI or DisplayPort cable or adapter. That is flexible, but less convenient if your monitors already have HDMI-only inputs and you want to avoid buying additional adapters.

 14-in-1 Thunderbolt 5 Dock: Equipped with a Thunderbolt 5 upstream port, two Thunderbolt 5 downstream ports, two USB-C ports, three USB-A ports, SD and TF card readers, an AC input, a 2.5Gbps Ethernet port, an audio jack, and an HDMI 2.1 or DisplayPort 2.1 port. It also includes an advanced active cooling system for optimal performance even under full load, preventing overheating.
 The Speed You Need for Large Files: Transfer massive files quickly-move a 150GB file in just 25 seconds with the Thunderbolt 5 port.
 Dual Display Docking Station: Supports one HDMI or DisplayPort and two Thunderbolt 5 downstream video outputs. Delivers up to 8K@60Hz for a single display, or dual 8K@60Hz for Thunderbolt 5 Windows laptops.
 Fast Charge Multiple Devices: Power your devices efficiently with the powerful 140W max Thunderbolt 5 upstream port, supporting the PD 3.1 protocol for optimal charging. The front-facing dual USB-C ports share a total of 45W.

 Retail pricing has been listed around $219.99, making it one of the less expensive ways to get native TB5 connectivity. Before buying, check the exact retailer listing and the display configuration you intend to use.
 6. Plugable UD-7400PD: best for exceeding Apple’s native display limit 
 The Plugable UD-7400PD solves a different problem from the other docks. It is a USB-C DisplayLink dock, not a Thunderbolt dock. It can support up to five external displays in supported configurations, including one HDMI 2.1 output, one HDMI 2.0 DisplayLink output and three USB-C DisplayLink outputs. Plugable rates it for up to five 4K/60Hz displays, up to 140W host charging, 30W device charging and 2.5Gb Ethernet.
 On macOS, install DisplayLink Manager and allow it under System Settings > Privacy & Security > Screen Recording . Some installations also require background activity permission. Without those permissions, displays may remain blank or fail to extend the desktop.
 DisplayLink is useful when a MacBook’s native display maximum is not enough, but it is not identical to native Thunderbolt video. It adds a software layer, and Plugable states that HDCP-protected content such as Netflix and Hulu is unsupported through the UD-7400PD’s DisplayLink outputs. Choose it for office productivity and multi-screen workflows—not as the default choice for a home-theater setup.
 Which dock matches your MacBook?

 DisplayLink, accepting its software and protected-video limitations. 
 The M5 MacBook Air’s two Thunderbolt 4 ports support charging, DisplayPort, Thunderbolt 4 and USB4 at up to 40Gbps. Apple lists support for two displays at up to 6K/60Hz or 4K/144Hz, or one display at up to 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz or 4K/240Hz in supported configurations. Closing the lid does not increase the Air’s external-display limit.
 For the 16-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro or M5 Max, Apple specifies a 140W-or-higher USB-C power source for fast charging. A dock does not have to provide 140W for the Mac to operate or charge, although higher-power delivery is useful for reducing battery drain during demanding work.
 USB-C and Thunderbolt buying traps 
 A USB-C plug does not define the dock’s capabilities
 USB-C describes the connector, not the complete protocol. A USB-C port may offer USB 2, USB 3, USB4, DisplayPort Alt Mode, Thunderbolt or only charging. For dock-connected video, the Mac’s port and the dock path must support the necessary display mode. “Works with USB-C” is therefore not enough information by itself.

 WAVLINK Intel EVO Certified Thunderbolt 5 Dock, 120Gbps, 140W PD, 8K | Thunderbolt 5 Docking Station hub TB5 Dock 8K Display 140W Max Charging 4X USB-A 3.2 TBT 5/4 Laptops laptop cooling system 
 [Pioneering Thunderbolt 5 Technology] – Experience the next frontier of connectivity with the latest Thunderbolt 5 technology dock. Delivering a staggering 120Gbps maximum transfer bandwidth (boost mode) and 140W Power Delivery to your laptop, this 12-in-1 station is engineered for elite professionals who demand unrivaled speed and high-wattage charging in one centralized hub.
 [Elite 8K Visuals & Triple Display Productivity] – Elevate your workspace with cinema-grade clarity. Support a single 8K@144Hz display or dual 8K@60Hz setups. Windows 11 users can unlock triple 4K@144Hz external displays for seamless multitasking in video production or trading. (Note: macOS supports dual external displays; triple display requires Windows 11 or later with a Thunderbolt 5 port.)
 [High-Speed Data Hub & Multi-Device Charging] – Beyond the 140W host charging, three downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports provide dedicated 15W & 30W PD to keep your phone and tablet powered simultaneously. Coupled with a 2.5G Ethernet port for lag-free networking and an SD 4.0 reader (312MB/s), it ensures your creative workflow remains uninterrupted.
 [Exquisite Design and Enhanced Security] – Carefully designed for a stable desktop experience, it features four non-slip pads to prevent accidental movement and a built-in Kensington lock slot for theft protection. Four USB-A 3.2 ports are strategically placed to connect your wireless mouse, keyboard, and other legacy peripherals without interference
 [Compatibility and Professional Support] – For optimal performance, your computer’s USB-C port must be compatible with Thunderbolt 4 or 5. Please note that the supported resolution and refresh rate depend on the host device’s specifications. (USB-C to HDMI/DP cables and security locks are not included.) Our dedicated technical team is available 24/7 to assist you with any setup questions.
 $219.99 
 Buy on Amazon 
 TB5 does not upgrade an M5 Air
 A Thunderbolt 5 dock is backward-compatible with Thunderbolt 4, but an M5 MacBook Air remains limited by its Thunderbolt 4 host connection. Buy TB5 for its port layout, charging capability, current accessories or future Mac—not for TB5 transfer speeds on the Air.
 An 8K label is not a promise for every Mac
 Dock and GPU limits interact. A dock may advertise 8K while a particular Mac, output or adapter path is limited to 6K or a lower refresh rate. Check the exact Mac chip, dock output, cable specification and monitor mode. Apple’s built-in HDMI port on some MacBook Pro configurations can also have capabilities that differ from a dock output.
 How to approve and configure a new dock 
 Identify the Mac by choosing Apple menu  > About This Mac . For more detail, open System Information and confirm the chip and model.
 Connect the dock while the Mac is unlocked. If macOS displays an accessory approval prompt, choose to allow it. If you selected Don’t Allow , the Mac may still charge while blocking data and displays.
 Review the setting at System Settings > Privacy & Security > Accessories > Allow accessories to connect . The choices include Always Ask , Ask for New Accessories , Automatically Allow When Unlocked and Always Allow .
 Configure monitors at System Settings > Displays . Select a display to change Resolution , Refresh Rate , Use as or Optimize for .
 If a screen is missing, hold Option in Displays settings to reveal Detect Displays , then select it.
 For a DisplayLink dock, install DisplayLink Manager, then go to System Settings > Privacy & Security > Screen Recording and enable DisplayLink Manager. Authenticate if requested, then choose Quit & Reopen .
 Dock troubleshooting that actually narrows the problem 
 It charges but nothing else works: reconnect while the Mac is unlocked and revisit Privacy & Security > Accessories . The accessory approval may have been denied.
 The monitor is black or stuck at a low refresh rate: test another cable, reduce the selected resolution or refresh rate, reconnect the display, sleep and wake the Mac, and use Detect Displays . A dock output or adapter may not support the requested mode.
 Closed-lid mode fails: connect the Mac to power and use an external keyboard and mouse. Approve the display, keyboard and mouse before closing the lid.
 DisplayLink works on Windows but not macOS: install DisplayLink Manager and grant Screen Recording permission.
 A streaming service is blank: protected HDCP video may not work through a DisplayLink output. Try a native Thunderbolt, HDMI or direct-to-Mac connection.
 10Gb Ethernet fails through USB4: on the TS5 Plus, that feature requires a Thunderbolt host or a USB4 host with PCIe support.
 A monitor works directly but not through the dock: connect it directly to the Mac as a diagnostic test. If it works there, investigate the dock output, adapter, cable, bandwidth or compatibility rather than the monitor first.
 FAQ 
 Is a Thunderbolt 5 dock worth buying for an M5 MacBook Air?
 Usually only for its port selection, high-power charging or future-proofing. The M5 MacBook Air has Thunderbolt 4 ports, so a TB5 dock will operate at the Air’s Thunderbolt 4 limits.
 Can an M5 MacBook Air run two monitors from a dock?
 Yes, within Apple’s supported display configurations. The Air supports up to two external displays, but a dock cannot increase that native limit. Closing the lid does not unlock additional displays.
 What is better for a MacBook: Thunderbolt or DisplayLink?
 Use native Thunderbolt when you want driver-free operation, predictable video behavior and protected streaming. Use DisplayLink when exceeding Apple’s native display count is more important than software dependencies and HDCP compatibility.
 Does a dock need to provide 140W to charge a MacBook Pro?
 No. A dock can charge and operate the Mac with less power. However, Apple requires a 140W-or-higher USB-C power source for fast charging the 16-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro or M5 Max.
 The Bottom Line 
 For an M5 MacBook Air or base-M5 MacBook Pro, spend on a well-equipped Thunderbolt 4 or USB-C dock unless you have a specific reason to choose TB5. For an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro, Thunderbolt 5 is the better long-term choice when the desk includes multiple high-resolution displays, fast external storage or 10Gb networking.
 Choose the CalDigit TS5 Plus for the broadest premium connectivity, the Plugable TBT-UDT3 for better TB5 value, the OWC Thunderbolt 5 Dock for mixed host compatibility, and the Anker Prime when built-in HDMI and DisplayPort matter most. Pick the Plugable UD-7400PD only when you genuinely need DisplayLink’s extra screens and accept its macOS permissions and HDCP limitations.

 Questions

 Is a dock with an SSD worth it? If you use one desk, yes: Time Machine backups and project files stay connected without an extra drive and cable. Check whether the SSD is built in or bring-your-own, the maximum capacity, and that the slot supports PCIe 4.0 for full speed.

 For Whom the Satechi TB4 Docking Station Is Good
 MacBook Air owners on base M1, M2, M3, or M4 chips who need multiple external displays. The DisplayLink integration is the cleanest we tested, and Satechi’s Space Gray design matches Apple hardware better than most third-party docks. The 96W charging is also enough for any MacBook Pro except the heaviest 16-inch workloads.
 Hybrid workers who split time between home and office will appreciate the slim chassis and included travel-friendly cable.
 For Whom the Satechi TB4 Docking Station Is Not Ideal
 If you do not need DisplayLink, the Plugable 16-in-1 or CalDigit TS4 deliver dual displays natively without driver installation. Buyers who need 2.5Gb Ethernet should look at the CalDigit, Sonnet, Plugable, or Dell docks. Only two USB-A ports is restrictive for full desktop setups.

 How to Choose the Best Thunderbolt 4 Dock for Your MacBook
 The best Thunderbolt 4 dock for MacBook depends on three things: your MacBook’s chip, your display count, and how much power delivery you need. Start there before you look at port counts or brand names.
 Thunderbolt 4 vs Thunderbolt 5 vs USB4
 Thunderbolt 4 delivers 40Gbps of total bandwidth, supports dual 4K@60Hz displays, requires 32Gbps PCIe tunneling for storage, and mandates at least one downstream Thunderbolt port. Thunderbolt 5 doubles that to 80Gbps, with 120Gbps in one direction for displays, and adds support for dual 8K displays. USB4 is a broader standard that ranges from 20Gbps to 80Gbps depending on the implementation. For most MacBook owners today, Thunderbolt 4 is the right sweet spot. Thunderbolt 5 is forward-looking, and Apple has not yet adopted it on MacBook Pro or Air as of 2026.
 Power Delivery: How Many Watts Your MacBook Needs
 Power Delivery (PD) is the wattage the dock sends back through the Thunderbolt cable to charge your MacBook. The 13-inch MacBook Air draws up to 35W, the 14-inch MacBook Pro up to 70W, and the 16-inch MacBook Pro up to 140W under heavy load. A 90W dock is fine for the Air and 14-inch Pro. For the 16-inch Pro, look for 100W or higher. The CalDigit TS4’s 98W and Sonnet Echo 20’s 100W are realistic upper limits for Thunderbolt 4 docks today.
 External Displays: What Your M-Series Chip Supports
 Apple silicon has a complicated display story. Base M1, M2, M3, and M4 chips support only one external display natively. M1 Pro, M2 Pro, M3 Pro, M4 Pro, M1 Max, M2 Max, M3 Max, M4 Max, M1 Ultra, M2 Ultra, M3 Ultra, and M4 Ultra chips support multiple displays. The CalDigit TS4 supports dual 6K@60Hz on Pro and Max chips. The iVANKY FusionDock Max 1 goes further to quad 6K@60Hz on Max and Ultra chips. The Satechi dock with DisplayLink is the workaround for base chips.
 M1 and M2 Single-Display Workaround with DisplayLink
 DisplayLink is a driver and compression technology that lets your MacBook output additional displays over USB. The Satechi Thunderbolt 4 Docking Station and the UGREEN dock both use DisplayLink chips. On a base M2 MacBook Air, you can run two 4K@60Hz external displays through DisplayLink. The downside is a third-party driver that occasionally breaks with macOS updates. For most office users it is a perfectly stable workaround.
 Hub vs Dock: What Do You Actually Need
 A hub is small, bus-powered or lightly powered, and adds basic ports. A dock is a larger brick with its own power supply, full charging passthrough, and more ports. If you want to charge your MacBook over a single cable while running external monitors and Ethernet, you need a dock. If you just need a couple more USB-A ports on the road, a hub like the OWC Thunderbolt Hub is enough.
 MacBook Compatibility Matrix
 MacBook Air M1, M2, M3, M4: native single display. Add DisplayLink for dual displays. MacBook Pro 13-inch M1, M2: native single display. MacBook Pro 14-inch M1 Pro, M2 Pro, M3 Pro, M4 Pro: native dual displays. MacBook Pro 16-inch M1 Pro, M2 Pro, M3 Pro, M4 Pro: native dual displays. MacBook Pro 14-inch and 16-inch M1 Max, M2 Max, M3 Max, M4 Max: native triple displays plus dock daisy-chain. Mac Studio M1 Ultra, M2 Ultra, M3 Ultra, M4 Ultra: native four displays plus dock daisy-chain.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best Thunderbolt 4 dock for MacBook?
 The CalDigit TS4 is the best Thunderbolt 4 dock for MacBook overall. It offers 18 ports including 98W charging, dual 6K@60Hz display support on M-series Pro and Max MacBook Pros, 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet, and rock-solid driverless macOS support. For dual displays on a base M1 or M2 MacBook Air, the Satechi Thunderbolt 4 Docking Station with DisplayLink is the better pick.
 Are Thunderbolt 4 docks worth it for a MacBook?
 Yes. Modern MacBooks ship with only two to four USB-C ports, which forces you to choose between charging, an external display, and a wired network connection. A Thunderbolt 4 dock turns your MacBook into a one-cable desktop, adds reliable Ethernet, supports one or more 4K or 6K monitors, and charges the laptop at the same time. For hybrid workers, content creators, and developers, a Thunderbolt 4 dock pays for itself in productivity within a few months.
 Do Thunderbolt 4 docks work with M4 and M5 MacBooks?
 Yes. Thunderbolt 4 is backwards compatible with Thunderbolt 3, USB4, and USB-C hosts. The M4 and M5 MacBook Pro and Air models all support Thunderbolt 4 or Thunderbolt 5 ports, and every dock in this guide works with them. Macs with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips can take full advantage of Thunderbolt 5 docks as well, though Thunderbolt 4 docks remain a strong value pick.
 How many monitors can a Thunderbolt 4 dock support on a MacBook?
 On MacBook Pro models with M1 Pro, M2 Pro, M3 Pro, M4 Pro, M1 Max, M2 Max, M3 Max, M4 Max, or any Ultra chip, a Thunderbolt 4 dock can drive two extended displays at up to 6K@60Hz each. The iVANKY FusionDock Max 1 goes further with dual Thunderbolt 4 chips for quad 6K@60Hz on Max and Ultra chips. On base M1, M2, M3, or M4 MacBook Air and 13-inch MacBook Pro models, you are limited to a single native display unless you add a DisplayLink dock.
 What is the difference between Thunderbolt 4 and USB4 docks?
 Thunderbolt 4 mandates 40Gbps bandwidth, dual 4K@60Hz display support, 32Gbps PCIe tunneling, and at least one downstream Thunderbolt port. USB4 is a broader standard that ranges from 20Gbps to 80Gbps depending on the implementation, and dock builders can pick and choose features. In practice, a certified Thunderbolt 4 dock is a safer buy because Intel certifies it meets a fixed feature set. USB4 docks can be excellent value but vary widely in real-world performance.
 Can I use a Thunderbolt 5 dock with a Thunderbolt 4 MacBook?
 Yes. Thunderbolt 5 is backwards compatible with Thunderbolt 4 and USB4 hosts. A Thunderbolt 5 dock will work with a current MacBook Pro or Air at Thunderbolt 4 speeds. The dock will not unlock Thunderbolt 5’s full 80Gbps bandwidth unless the host also supports Thunderbolt 5. As of 2026, no MacBook Pro or MacBook Air ships with Thunderbolt 5, so a Thunderbolt 5 dock is forward-looking rather than immediately useful.
 The Bottom Line: Our Final Pick for the Best Thunderbolt 4 Dock for MacBook
 After three months of testing with three different MacBook models, the CalDigit TS4 remains the best Thunderbolt 4 dock for MacBook owners in 2026. It delivers the strongest combination of port selection, charging headroom, dual 6K display support, and firmware reliability. The Plugable 16-in-1 is the right pick if you want real value, and the iVANKY FusionDock Max 1 is the only choice for quad-display MacBook Pro setups. If you are still on a base M1 or M2 MacBook Air, the Satechi Thunderbolt 4 Docking Station with DisplayLink is the cleanest workaround for multi-display workflows.
 Whichever dock you pick, the important thing is that you stop juggling dongles. Plug one cable into your MacBook, walk away from your desk, come back, plug in once, and your external monitors, Ethernet, SD card reader, and laptop charging all light up together. That is the entire point of a Thunderbolt 4 dock for MacBook, and every product on this list delivers it.

The correct choice depends less on the number of ports than on whether the dock’s display technology matches the Air’s chip and whether the dock supplies the bandwidth and connections your workflow actually uses.
